clinicalPearls: Typically presents as a unilateral, mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly and sluggishly to light in a young woman
The pupil shows light-near dissociation with a slow, tonic constriction to a sustained near effort and a slow tonic redilation afterwards
Slit-lamp examination often reveals segmental (vermiform) movements of the iris with sectors that fail to contract
Denervation supersensitivity means dilute pilocarpine constricts the affected pupil but not a normal one, confirming the diagnosis pharmacologically
Diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes together with a tonic pupil constitutes Holmes-Adie syndrome
Over time the affected pupil may become smaller than the fellow pupil (the 'little old Adie's pupil')
The condition is usually benign and idiopathic, thought to follow damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves
reference.pathophysiology: Adie tonic pupil results from damage to the parasympathetic ciliary ganglion or the short ciliary nerves, interrupting postganglionic innervation to the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle. Aberrant regeneration favours the far more numerous accommodative fibres over the pupillary fibres, so the pupil constricts poorly to light but responds tonically during the near reflex, producing light-near dissociation. Loss of innervation leads to denervation supersensitivity of the sphincter, which underlies the constriction to dilute cholinergic drops. The cause is usually idiopathic, sometimes following viral illness or local orbital injury.
additionalDifferentials: Pharmacological mydriasis from topical or systemic anticholinergic exposure
Third nerve palsy with pupil involvement
Acute angle closure with a fixed mid-dilated pupil
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination for segmental iris palsy and vermiform movements
Dilute pilocarpine testing to demonstrate cholinergic supersensitivity
Assessment of deep tendon reflexes for Holmes-Adie syndrome
Serological testing for syphilis where light-near dissociation is present
Autonomic function assessment when widespread dysautonomia is suspected
Neuroimaging only if atypical features suggest a compressive third nerve lesion
redFlags: A dilated pupil with ptosis and ocular motility deficit suggesting a compressive third nerve palsy
Acute painful red eye with a fixed pupil suggesting angle-closure glaucoma
Bilateral light-near dissociation raising the possibility of neurosyphilis or midbrain disease
Associated widespread autonomic failure needing further evaluation
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign; acuity is unaffected once accommodation adapts, though the pupil generally remains abnormal and may become progressively miotic, and any accompanying areflexia is permanent but harmless.
pitfalls: Mistaking a tonic pupil for a compressive third nerve palsy and initiating unnecessary urgent imaging
Overlooking the near response and labelling the pupil simply as fixed and dilated
Failing to consider neurosyphilis when dissociation is bilateral
Not recognising pharmacological mydriasis, which fails to constrict even to standard pilocarpine
management: Reassure regarding the benign nature and preserved visual acuity once accommodation adapts
Offer dilute pilocarpine drops to improve cosmesis and ease accommodative symptoms and photophobia
Prescribe near optical correction for accommodative difficulty and tinted or photochromic lenses for photophobia
Exclude syphilis with serological testing where light-near dissociation is present
Assess deep tendon reflexes and consider autonomic evaluation, recognising Holmes-Adie syndrome
Refer to neuro-ophthalmology, reserving neuroimaging for atypical features suggesting a compressive third-nerve lesion
